---
title: "Stage 7 — compare against what was built"
---

The stage that tells you whether any of it was right.

## What this is

Here, the study already had analysis datasets built by a programmer working from the same plan.
Comparing the executed result against them is the strongest external check available, because
the two implementations are genuinely independent.

**Most readers will not have that, and it is worth being clear about why.** An independently
built implementation exists when someone has already done the work by hand. That is true of a
study being re-examined, and false of one being specified for the first time. On a new study
there is nothing to compare against, and in the world these standards aim at there is nothing
to compare against *by design*: the point of a declared specification is to stop having two
implementations that must be reconciled.

So this stage is partly transitional. It is most useful now, while both worlds exist.

**What to do instead, when there is nothing to compare against.** Reproduce the engine's number
outside the engine, using the engine's own selection: the filters and joins its console
reported at stage 6. That is a weaker check than an independent implementation, because it
shares the engine's assumptions. But it is the check that actually found the mechanism
described below — not by disagreeing with the answer, but by making the engine's choices
explicit enough to see.

## What you do

**The work:** fit the same model on the study's own derived variables, and explain every part
of any difference.

1. Fit the same model on the study's own derived variables.
2. Compare the two results.
3. Where they disagree, reproduce the engine's number outside the engine, using the engine's
   own selection.
4. Sort each cause of the difference into a class.

## What you should see

Two numbers that do not match, and an explanation for every part of the gap. Each engine result
should be reproducible to four decimals once its selection is known.

Here they are for both analyses, at Cycle 2 Day 1 (`C2D1` in the data), on the data this book
is fixed to. The reference in each case is the same model fitted on the study's own derived
variables: its change, its baseline, its analysis-record flag. The count is the number of
subjects for whom the engine's baseline record is not the one the study's flag marks. Every
figure is read from the runs.

| Laboratory, ANCOVA at C2D1 | |
|---|---|
| Engine, placebo minus torivumab | {{fact:lab.engine.diff|4}} (SE {{fact:lab.contrast.se|3}}) |
| Reference, same model on the study's variables | {{fact:lab.reference.diff|4}} (SE {{fact:lab.reference.se|3}}) |
| Subjects whose baseline record differs | {{fact:lab.baseline.differ}} of {{fact:lab.baseline.subjects}} |

| Blood pressure, MMRM at C2D1 | |
|---|---|
| Engine, placebo minus torivumab | {{fact:vitals.mmrm.c2d1.estimate|4}} (SE {{fact:vitals.mmrm.c2d1.se|3}}) |
| Reference, same model on the study's variables | {{fact:vitals.mmrm.c2d1.reference|4}} (SE {{fact:vitals.mmrm.c2d1.reference.se|3}}) |
| Subjects whose baseline record differs | {{fact:vitals.baseline.differ}} of {{fact:vitals.baseline.subjects}} |

The second gap is the larger. The repeated-measures model is not what makes it so: the same
endpoint under an ANCOVA at that one visit shows a gap of the same size, and the vitals
comparison record has both. What the repeated-measures model changes is how far the baseline
reaches. It enters the change at every visit, so every visit's contrast moves, not one.

### Step into the factory

The comparisons are `comparison.md` in `endpoints/01-simple-lab-cfb/` and
`endpoints/04-vitals-cfb-mmrm/`, each with the reference fit, the replica of the engine's
selection outside the engine, and the classification of every cause. The subject counts come
from `tools/check_baseline_ambiguity.py`, run against the study's data. The three classes a
divergence is sorted into are set in `docs/specification.md`.

## What to look out for

**A divergence is a result, not a failure, but only if you can explain all of it.** The
mechanism here is a disagreement over the baseline record, and it is worth stating as a rule
rather than a symptom. The plan defines baseline *by date*: the last value on or before the
first dose. The chain declares it *by visit*: the record at the Baseline visit. A subject with a
screening draw and a pre-dose draw on day one has two records at that visit, and the two rules
pick different ones. The study's flag marks the later; the engine takes the first it finds. It
affects most subjects in both analyses.

Explaining all of it means sorting every cause into one of three classes. An **authoring
error** is one the chain could have been authored to get right: a wrong covariate, a dimension
in the wrong form. A **model limitation** is one no authoring fixes: here, the chain can state
the visit but not which record in it. A **specification ambiguity** is one where the plan
itself admits two readings. This analysis had none of the third, since the plan was precise.

**Reproduce before you conclude.** A gap you cannot reproduce outside the engine is not yet
understood, and the temptation to call it a rounding difference is strong and usually wrong.
